summary:
Same-sex relations are not criminalised in Cabo Verde, and the country's employment discrimination prohibition covers sexual orientation. The protection does not extend to gender identity, leaving trans visitors and residents without an explicit statutory basis for workplace complaints (Outright International, updated 12 March 2026).

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. As of 2016 civil law blocked Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed trans woman in Cabo Verde, from changing her legal name to a female one; the source inventory contains no later statute or administrative route for legal gender change.

Same-sex unions are not recognised. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva stated on 11 July 2017 that same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, following LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Public visibility is high by regional standards. Cabo Verde held its first public Pride in 2013, the second African country to do so. The 2018 Pride Week in Praia combined a parade with campaigns by the Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, the Associação LGBTI de Praia and the Associação Arco Iris, which petitioned the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; the gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women took part. Polling in 2019–21 found 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour.

Trans-specific violence is documented at individual level rather than as a recorded pattern. Tchinda Andrade, who came out in 1997 at age 19, described Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, but reported verbal violence and two physical attacks against her. The inventory contains no case series, prosecution record or official count of anti-trans violence.
tangentialFactors:
Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020) places Cabo Verde alongside Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe as particularly tolerant African countries, while finding that tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak across the continent even among younger respondents. The same survey frames tolerance on ethnic, religious and national differences as broadly high, which is not the same measure as acceptance of sexual difference.

Cabo Verde is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group and made anti-discrimination commitments under the Universal Periodic Review in 2024. LGBTIQ organisations register freely in the country. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva's 2017 remark distancing himself from MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro's opposition to same-sex marriage indicates division within the governing party rather than a settled legislative position.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered by an employment discrimination prohibition that names sexual orientation, giving a domestic legal basis for workplace complaints on that ground. No equivalent gender-identity ground is stated in the sources.

Domestic partners have no route to legal recognition of a same-sex union, so inheritance, hospital visitation and next-of-kin questions are governed by default civil law rather than partnership status.

LGBTIQ organisations operate openly and register without restriction, and the national gender-equality institute ICIEG engages with Pride programming. Advocacy groups including the Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, the Associação LGBTI de Praia and the Associação Arco Iris petition the National Assembly directly.

Public acceptance is measurable: 82% of respondents in 2019–21 polling said they would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour, and the country has held public Pride events annually since 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any administrative practice permits a gender or name marker change on identity documents is unresolved. The only sourced statement is Tchinda Andrade's 2016 account that civil law blocked her name change; no later legal or administrative status is in the inventory.

Enforcement of the employment discrimination protection is not sourced. The inventory states the prohibition exists and that it covers sexual orientation, but records no complaint outcomes, labour-inspectorate practice or court decisions.

Hate-crime or aggravated-penalty provisions covering anti-trans motivation are not sourced either way. The absence of such a provision in the inventory is not evidence that none exists.

The scale of anti-trans violence beyond Tchinda Andrade's reported verbal abuse and two physical attacks is not sourced. No police statistics, NGO incident counts or court records are available here, so the assessment of low documented risk rests on a single first-person account plus the absence of a recorded pattern.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans travellers, including how gender markers on passports are treated at arrival, are not covered by any source in this inventory.
